title: Input with read, Output with printf
summary: Read lines of input into variables with read, and print values in exactly the format you want with printf.
intro: So far your scripts worked on files and on values written into the code. Most real scripts also take input: a name someone types, or lines piped in from another command. `read` takes one line from stdin and splits it into variables, and `printf` prints values in exactly the format you choose. From this lesson on, a practice can have several tests, and each one feeds your script a different input on stdin. To try an input yourself, type it in the stdin box under the editor before you press Run. The folder your script runs in also holds this lesson's files, like `hosts.txt` and `build/VERSION`.

steps.title: Read a line
steps.body:
`read` takes one line from stdin and stores it in a variable. Always write `-r`: without it, `read` treats a backslash as an escape character and drops it.

```stdin
Ada Lovelace
```

```bash
read -r name
echo "Hello, $name!"
```

Give `read` several names and it splits the line into words, on spaces and tabs. Each name gets one word, and the last name gets everything left over:

```stdin
web-1 10.0.0.5 eu-west production
```

```bash
read -r host ip rest
echo "$host is at $ip, rest: $rest"
```

`IFS` holds the characters `read` splits on. Set it right before the command, as in `IFS=, read -r a b`, and it changes for that one `read` only.

`read` can also take a line from a file with `<`. When there's no line left to read, it exits 1, so it works as a test:

```bash
read -r version < build/VERSION
echo "version $version"
read -r first < empty.txt || echo "empty.txt has no lines"
```

examples.title: One value per line
examples.prompt: Read a name and an age, one per line, and greet the person.
examples.code:
read -r name
read -r age
echo "Hello, $name!"
echo "In 10 years you'll be $(( age + 10 ))."
examples.output:
Hello, Ada!
In 10 years you'll be 46.
examples.explanation: Each `read` takes the next line of stdin, so `name` gets `Ada` and `age` gets `36`. `read` stores text, but `$(( ))` reads `36` as a number, so the age plus 10 prints as 46. Change the input in the stdin box and press Run to see the output follow it.

examples.title: The last name takes the rest
examples.prompt: Split a full name into its first word and the rest, then split a line that has fewer words than names.
examples.code:
read -r first rest
echo "first: $first"
echo "rest: $rest"

read -r a b c d
echo "a=$a b=$b c=$c d=[$d]"
examples.stdin:
Grace Brewster Hopper
  x   y  z
examples.output:
first: Grace
rest: Brewster Hopper
a=x b=y c=z d=[]
examples.explanation: `read` splits on spaces. `first` takes the first word, and `rest`, the last name given, takes everything after it, the space between `Brewster` and `Hopper` included. The second line starts with spaces and has runs of spaces between its words: a run counts as one separator, and spaces at the ends are dropped. It has three words for four names, so `d` stays empty.

examples.title: Commas and backslashes
examples.prompt: Split a line on commas, then read the same Windows path with and without `-r`.
examples.code:
IFS=, read -r city temp
echo "$city: $temp degrees"

read -r path
echo "with -r: $path"
read path
echo "without -r: $path"
examples.output:
Lisbon: 21 degrees
with -r: C:\temp\new
without -r: C:tempnew
examples.explanation: `IFS=,` before `read` makes the comma the separator for that one command, so `city` is `Lisbon` and `temp` is `21`. The next two lines hold the same path. With `-r`, `read` keeps every backslash. Without it, a backslash escapes the character after it and disappears, so the path comes out as `C:tempnew`. That's why every `read` you write should have `-r`.

practice.title: Next birthday
practice.prompt:
Read a name and an age from one line of input, and say how old the person turns next.

1. Read the line into `name` and `age` with one `read -r`.
2. Print `Hi NAME, next year you'll be N`, where N is the age plus 1.

Input:

```text
Ada 36
```

Expected output:

```text
Hi Ada, next year you'll be 37
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: read the name and the age from one line

# TODO: print the greeting with the age plus 1
practice.solution:
read -r name age
echo "Hi $name, next year you'll be $(( age + 1 ))"

tests.output: Hi Ada, next year you'll be 37
Hi Linus, next year you'll be 57
Hi Grace, next year you'll be 86

hints: One `read -r name age` splits the line: the first word goes to `name`, and the rest to `age`.
`$(( age + 1 ))` adds one. The apostrophe in `you'll` is fine inside double quotes.

steps.title: Format output with printf
steps.body:
`printf FORMAT ARGUMENTS...` prints its arguments in the shape the format gives. In the format, `%s` stands for a string and `%d` for a whole number. `printf` never adds a newline by itself, so end the format with `\n`:

```bash
printf '%s has %d hosts\n' web 3
```

Between the `%` and the letter go a width and a precision. `%8s` pads to 8 characters on the left, `%-8s` pads on the right, `%05d` pads with zeros, and `%.2f` keeps 2 decimals. `%%` prints a percent sign:

```bash
printf '[%8s] [%-8s] [%05d] [%.2f] 100%%\n' tea tea 42 3.14159
```

When there are more arguments than the format uses, `printf` runs the format again for the rest, which turns a list into lines:

```bash
printf '%s\n' web-1 web-2 db-1
```

In scripts, prefer `printf` to `echo -e` and `echo -n`, because shells disagree on what `echo` does with options and backslashes. On this system `sh` is dash, not Bash, and its `echo` prints the `-e` as text. `printf` gives the same result in both:

```bash
printf 'a\tb\n'
echo -e 'a\tb'
sh -c "echo -e 'a\tb'"
```

examples.title: Widths and decimals
examples.prompt: Print a sentence, then a few padded fields between brackets to show where each one starts and ends.
examples.code:
printf '%s is %d years old\n' Ada 36
printf '[%-8s|%6.2f]\n' tea 3.5
printf '[%8s|%-6d|%05d]\n' coffee 42 42
examples.explanation: Each `%` spec takes the next argument in order. `%-8s` pads `tea` to 8 characters with spaces after it, and `%6.2f` prints 3.5 with 2 decimals, padded to 6 characters on the left. Without the minus, `%8s` pads on the left, so `coffee` lines up on the right. `%-6d` puts 42 on the left of its 6 characters, and `%05d` fills them with zeros instead of spaces.

examples.title: A table from input
examples.prompt: Read two items and their prices, then print them as a table under a header.
examples.code:
read -r item1 price1
read -r item2 price2

printf '%-8s %6s\n' item price
printf '%-8s %6.2f\n' "$item1" "$price1" "$item2" "$price2"
examples.explanation: The header and the rows use the same widths, so the columns line up: names padded to 8 on the right, prices to 6 on the left. The second `printf` gets four arguments for a format that uses two, so it runs the format twice, once per row. `%6.2f` also gives both prices the same 2 decimals, so `3.5` prints as `3.50`.

examples.title: Dollars from cents
examples.prompt: Build strings with `printf -v` instead of printing them: a padded ticket number and a price kept in cents.
examples.code:
printf -v padded '%03d' 7
echo "ticket-$padded"

cents=1205
printf -v price '%d.%02d' $(( cents / 100 )) $(( cents % 100 ))
echo "price: $price"

printf 'paid: 100%%\n'
examples.explanation: `printf -v padded` stores the result in `padded` instead of printing it, so `padded` holds `007`. Money is often kept in cents, a whole number, so Bash's math can work on it. `cents / 100` is 12, the dollars, and `cents % 100` is 5, the cents. `%02d` pads the cents to two digits, so 5 becomes `05` and the price reads `12.05`. With `%d.%d`, it would read `12.5`. The last line shows `%%`, a literal percent sign.

practice.title: Receipt
practice.prompt:
Print a receipt for two items. Each input line holds an item name, a quantity, and a unit price in cents.

1. Read the two lines with `read -r`.
2. For each item, work out its total in cents, the quantity times the price.
3. Turn each total into dollars with `printf -v` and `%d.%02d`.
4. Print each item with the format `%-10s x%-3d %8s\n`: the name, the quantity, and the dollars.
5. Print the last line with the format `%-15s %8s\n`: the word `TOTAL` and the sum of both totals in dollars.

Input:

```text
tea 2 350
cookies 3 125
```

Expected output:

```text
tea        x2       7.00
cookies    x3       3.75
TOTAL              10.75
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: read the two lines: item, quantity, and price in cents

# TODO: work out each item's total in cents, and the sum of both

# TODO: turn each total and the sum into dollars with printf -v and %d.%02d

# TODO: print both items with '%-10s x%-3d %8s\n', then TOTAL with '%-15s %8s\n'
practice.solution:
read -r item1 qty1 cents1
read -r item2 qty2 cents2

total1=$(( qty1 * cents1 ))
total2=$(( qty2 * cents2 ))
sum=$(( total1 + total2 ))

printf -v dollars1 '%d.%02d' $(( total1 / 100 )) $(( total1 % 100 ))
printf -v dollars2 '%d.%02d' $(( total2 / 100 )) $(( total2 % 100 ))
printf -v dollars '%d.%02d' $(( sum / 100 )) $(( sum % 100 ))

printf '%-10s x%-3d %8s\n' "$item1" "$qty1" "$dollars1"
printf '%-10s x%-3d %8s\n' "$item2" "$qty2" "$dollars2"
printf '%-15s %8s\n' TOTAL "$dollars"
hints: Give the second line its own names: `read -r item1 qty1 cents1`, then `read -r item2 qty2 cents2`.
`$(( qty1 * cents1 ))` is a total in cents. `printf -v dollars1 '%d.%02d' $(( total1 / 100 )) $(( total1 % 100 ))` turns 700 into `7.00`.
Add the two totals in cents first, then format the sum the same way for the TOTAL line.

steps.title: Prompts, secrets and defaults
steps.body:
Scripts that people run by hand ask before they read. `-p` shows a prompt, `-s` hides what's typed, for passwords, and `-t SECONDS` stops waiting after that long. The options combine, with `p` last because the prompt text follows it:

```stdin
Ada
s3cret
yes
```

```bash
read -rp "Name: " name
read -rsp "Password: " pw
read -r -t 5 answer
echo "$name, ${#pw} characters, $answer"
```

`read` writes its prompt to stderr, and only when the input comes from a terminal. On Run and Check, stdin is piped in, so the prompts never print and the output stays clean.

When there is no line left, `read` fails and leaves its variable empty, so a fallback after `||` gives it a default. Here stdin is empty:

```bash
read -r answer || answer="no"
echo "answer: $answer"
```

An empty line is different: `read` succeeds and stores nothing. `${answer:-no}` covers both cases.

examples.title: Prompts stay hidden
examples.prompt: Ask for a name and a city with prompts, then greet the person.
examples.code:
read -rp "Name: " name
read -rp "City: " city
echo "Hi $name from $city"
examples.explanation: In a terminal, you'd see `Name: ` and wait for your answer, then `City: `. Here the input comes from the stdin box, not a terminal, so `read` skips both prompts and the output is only the greeting. Check feeds your script the same way, which is why a practice never expects a prompt in its output.

examples.title: A hidden password
examples.prompt: Read a password without showing it, then print its length and a masked copy.
examples.explanation: In a terminal, `-s` keeps the typed characters off the screen. The Enter key doesn't show either, so the cursor stays on the prompt's line, and the bare `echo` moves it down. It writes to stderr, like the prompt, so stdout holds only the real output. `${#pw}` is the length, 7. In `${pw//?/*}`, `?` matches any one character and `//` replaces every match, so each character becomes a `*`.

examples.title: Defaults for missing input
examples.prompt: Read three answers, falling back to `no`, from input that has one answer, then an empty line, then nothing.
examples.code:
read -r -t 1 first || first="no"
echo "first: $first"

read -r -t 1 second || second="no"
echo "second: [$second]"
echo "second with a default: ${second:-no}"

read -r -t 1 third || third="no"
echo "third: $third"
examples.output:
first: yes
second: []
second with a default: no
third: no
examples.explanation: The first `read` gets `yes`. The second gets the empty line: that's still a line, so `read` succeeds, `||` never runs, and `second` is empty. `${second:-no}` catches that case. The third finds no line at all, so `read` fails and `||` sets `no`. `-t 1` would give up after a second if nobody typed, but here all the input is there at once, so it never waits.

practice.title: Sign-up form
practice.prompt:
Read a sign-up form from three lines of input and print what to save.

1. Read the username, the email, and the password, one line each. Give each `read` a prompt with `-p`, hide the password with `-s`, and after it end the prompt's line on stderr, as the hidden password example does.
2. Print `user=NAME`. An empty username line means `guest`.
3. Print `domain=DOMAIN`, the part of the email after the `@`.
4. Print `password=` followed by one `*` for each character of the password.

Input:

```text
ada
ada@shop.example
hunter22
```

Expected output:

```text
user=ada
domain=shop.example
password=********
```
practice.starter:
# TODO: read the username, the email, and the password with prompts

# TODO: print user=, with guest for an empty username

# TODO: print domain=, the part of the email after the @

# TODO: print password= and one * per character
practice.solution:
read -rp "Username: " user
read -rp "Email: " email
read -rsp "Password: " pw
echo >&2

echo "user=${user:-guest}"
echo "domain=${email#*@}"
echo "password=${pw//?/*}"
hints: Three `read` lines, one per field: `-rp` for the first two, and `-rsp` for the password followed by `echo >&2`. A plain `echo` would put an empty line at the top of your output.
`${user:-guest}` gives `guest` for an empty line, and `${email#*@}` drops everything up to and including the `@`.

recap:
- `read -r name` reads one line of stdin into `name`. Always use `-r`, so backslashes survive.
- With several names, `read` splits the line on spaces and tabs, and the last name takes the rest. `IFS=, read -r a b` splits on commas for that one command.
- `read` exits 1 when no line is left, so `read -r x || x=default` sets a fallback, and `${x:-default}` also covers an empty line.
- `-p` shows a prompt on stderr, only on a terminal. `-s` hides typing, and `-t N` stops waiting after N seconds.
- `printf` prints exactly its format: `%s`, `%d`, `%.2f`, widths like `%-10s` and `%8s`, zero padding with `%05d`, and `%%` for a percent sign. It adds no newline unless you write `\n`.
- Extra arguments run the format again, and `printf -v var` stores the result instead of printing it.
